messages.subject: Incomplete estimates from occuMulti?
parts:
Good evening,

I study the interaction between grazing species, before more complicate models I first will do a model with two species.

Formatting data into the unmarkedframe is easy,
but I do not understand some things following, I think it's because I only have experience with Occu (for single species), which is much different.

I copy below with questions;
umf <- unmarkedFrameOccuMulti(listo,siteCovs = covs,obsCovs = NULL)
summary(umf)
95 sites
2 species: sp1 sp2
Maximum number of observations per site: 11
Mean number of observations per site:
sp1: 9.71578947368421  sp2: 9.71578947368421  
Sites with at least one detection:
sp1: 63  sp2: 29  
etc.

Then I need to provide 'detformulas' and 'stateformulas' but I find it confusing:
I have 4  site variables and I want to study effect of variables on (co-)occupancy, I have no detection variables (for now).
so intuition tells me:
occForm <- c('~var1','~var2','~var3','~var4')
detForm <- c('~1','~1`)
Which is the variables for occupancy, and no detection variable for either species (2x ~1)
But function documentation says:
# Length should match number/order of columns in fDesign
so
> fm <- occuMulti(detForm,occForm,umf)
Error in .local(umf, ...) : 3 formulas are required in stateformulas list 

For me:
> umf[@]fDesign
        f1[sp1] f2[sp2] f3[sp1:sp2]
psi[11]       1       1           1
psi[10]       1       0           0
psi[01]       0       1           0
psi[00]       0       0           0
So what is the meaning of this? That I can only include 3 site covariates? 
If I do this, code runs, despite warning for +20 missing detection sites:
occForm <- c('~var1','~var2','~var3')
detForm <- c('~1','~1`)

But even now I do not have all covariates I want in model, estimates seem 'incomplete'?
Occupancy (logit-scale):
                                      Estimate     SE            z     P(>|z|)
[sp1] (Intercept)       0.8492       0.8968    0.947      0.3436
I think this is occupancy estimate just for SP1, without variables or interaction with SP2?
[sp1] var1                 -0.0021       0.0112   -0.188      0.8511
Ok, but where are estimates for SP1 in relation to var2 and var3?
[sp2] (Intercept)       2.4249       6.3518    0.382      0.7026
[sp2] var2                -2.5174       4.0836    -0.616      0.5376
Where are estimates for SP2 in relation to var1 and var3?
[sp1:sp2] (Intercept)  -8.6237  5.8416    -1.476     0.1399
I think this is estimate of the relation between species regarding their occupancy estimates? (neg interaction estimate, but non-significant)
[sp1:sp2] var3          5.9214      3.5237     1.680     0.0929
Where are estimates for relation between species in regard to var1 and var2?
Detection (logit-scale):
                  Estimate    SE      z  P(>|z|)
[sp1] (Intercept)    -1.23 0.106 -11.59 4.68e-31
[sp2] (Intercept)    -1.23 0.154  -7.98 1.42e-15
Not sure what these mean when I do not include observation covariates.

I want to thank greatly anyone who could give help on interpretation, I cannot find much information about occuMulti online, besides function documentation.

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incomplete estimates from occuMulti?
parts:
Formulas for occuMulti follow the same standards as normal R formulas. So if you want to model the effect of two covariates on one parameter, the relevant formula would be '~var1 + var2'.

In a normal occupancy model you only have two 'submodels', one for detection and one for occupancy. But for this model you have >2. Specifically, you have a submodel for every natural parameter (i.e. 'f' parameter) associated with occupancy, and one detection model per species. When you have two species, there are 3 f parameters (corresponding to species 1, species 2, and the species1:species2 interaction) associated with occupancy, hence the requirement for 3 formulas that you see. But each formula/submodel can have multiple covariates associated with it, as specified above.

If you look further down in the example for occuMulti, under #update, you will see an example of this. Also, see the attached vignette for a more detailed overview of the function. Results from this model can be tricky to interpret and it is important to have a good understanding of what each natural parameter represents before trying to make conclusions. I'd recommend reading the Rota 2016 paper and, if possible, Chapter 8 in Kéry & Royle's Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology Vol 2.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incomplete estimates from occuMulti?
parts:
Rota et al (2016) paper and chapter 8 of the book help a lot,
but there is no discussion for interpretation of p-values / significance. 

Can p-values be interpreted the same as we normally do? 
I would say:
                                           Est             SE          P
[Roe:Fallow] (Intercept)    0.956   0.468    0.065

probabylity of co-occupancy for the deer species is estimated higher than expected randomly, but P-value tells us the effect is non-significant (> 0.05).

but hard to interpret:  Est     SE           P
[Roe] (Intercept)            0.547  0.3257    0.0453
[Fallow] (Intercept)       -1.378  0.403      0.0141
 Probability of occupancy is estimated much higher for roe deer than for fallow deer, but  how can I interpret the P?
Similar, for p-values of detection variables , it is hard to interpret p-values relating to only ('intercept').

Thank you

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incomplete estimates from occuMulti?
parts:
I would just say

"We did not find evidence that the two species were more likely to co-occur at the same sites."

As for the individual species intercept p-values, you are testing if the value of these intercepts is statistically different from 0. This is an interesting test for the interaction term, but isn't usually useful for the single-species intercepts. If you want to compare overall occupancy between species I recommend calculating the marginal occupancy probabilities of each species and 95% confidence intervals using the predict() function as discussed in the vignette.

Ken

When you have two species, there are 3 f parameters (corresponding to species 1, species 2, and the species1:species2 interaction) associated with occupancy, hence the requirement for 3 formulas that you see. But each formula/submodel can have multiple covariates associated with it, as specified above.

If you look further down in the example for occuMulti, under #update, you will see an example of this. Also, see the attached vignette for a more detailed overview of the function. Results from this model can be tricky to interpret and it is important to have a good understanding of what each natural parameter represents before trying to make conclusions. I'd recommend reading the Rota 2016 paper and, if possible, Chapter 8 in Kéry & Royle's Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology Vol 2.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Incomplete estimates from occuMulti?
parts:
Hi Ken,
I've been trying to use your PDF to learn how to do multispecies occupancy models using unmarked, but it keeps telling me that the dataset MesoCarnivores was not found. I already updated R as well as unmarked to the newest version, but it didn't help. 
Any chance you could share the dataset with me? 
Thank you very much!
Annika

Ken Kellner schrieb am Mittwoch, 23. November 2022 um 14:00:42 UTC+1:
I would just say

"We did not find evidence that the two species were more likely to co-occur at the same sites."

As for the individual species intercept p-values, you are testing if the value of these intercepts is statistically different from 0. This is an interesting test for the interaction term, but isn't usually useful for the single-species intercepts. If you want to compare overall occupancy between species I recommend calculating the marginal occupancy probabilities of each species and 95% confidence intervals using the predict() function as discussed in the vignette.

Ken

[Roe:Fallow] (Intercept)    0.956   0.468    0.065

probabylity of co-occupancy for the deer species is estimated higher than expected randomly, but P-value tells us the effect is non-significant (> 0.05).

but hard to interpret:  Est     SE           P
[Roe] (Intercept)            0.547  0.3257    0.0453

 Probability of occupancy is estimated much higher for roe deer than for fallow deer, but  how can I interpret the P?
Similar, for p-values of detection variables , it is hard to interpret p-values relating to only ('intercept').

Thank you

Ken Kellner schrieb am Donnerstag, 24. November 2022 um 14:42:03 UTC+1:
The MesoCarnivores dataset can be found in the AHMbook R package. It will also be included with unmarked in the next CRAN release.

Ken

On Thu, Nov 24, 2022 at 12:29:28AM -0800, Annika Zuleger wrote:
> Hi Ken,
> I've been trying to use your PDF to learn how to do multispecies occupancy
> models using unmarked, but it keeps telling me that the dataset
> MesoCarnivores was not found. I already updated R as well as unmarked to
> the newest version, but it didn't help.
> Any chance you could share the dataset with me?
> Thank you very much!
> Annika
>
> Ken Kellner schrieb am Mittwoch, 23. November 2022 um 14:00:42 UTC+1:
>
> > I would just say
> >
> > "We did not find evidence that the two species were more likely to
> > co-occur at the same sites."
> >
> > As for the individual species intercept p-values, you are testing if the
> > value of these intercepts is statistically different from 0. This is an
> > interesting test for the interaction term, but isn't usually useful for the
> > single-species intercepts. If you want to compare overall occupancy between
> > species I recommend calculating the marginal occupancy probabilities of
> > each species and 95% confidence intervals using the predict() function as
> > discussed in the vignette.
> >
> > Ken
> >
> > On Tuesday, November 22, 2022 at 9:39:59 PM UTC-5 blaise...@gmail.com
> > wrote:
> >
> >>
> >> Rota et al (2016) paper and chapter 8 of the book help a lot,
> >> but there is no discussion for interpretation of p-values / significance.
> >>
> >> Can p-values be interpreted the same as we normally do?
> >> I would say:
> >>
> >>
> >> * Est SE P[Roe:Fallow] (Intercept)
> >> 0.956 0.468 0.065*
> >> probabylity of co-occupancy for the deer species is estimated higher than
> >> expected randomly, but P-value tells us the effect is non-significant (>
> >> 0.05).
> >>
> >> but hard to interpret:
> >>
> >> *Est SE P[Roe] (Intercept) 0.547 0.3257
> >> 0.0453[Fallow] (Intercept) -1.378 0.403 0.0141*
> >> Probability of occupancy is estimated much higher for roe deer than for
> >> fallow deer, but how can I interpret the P?
> >> Similar, for p-values of detection variables , it is hard to interpret
> >> p-values relating to only ('intercept').
> >>
> >> Thank you
> >>
> >> Op di 22 nov. 2022 om 17:03 schreef D. Blaise <blaise...@gmail.com>:
> >>
> >>> Thank you kindly, also for the PDF, this will help me so much!
> >>>
> >>> Op di 22 nov. 2022 om 15:44 schreef Ken Kellner <con...@kenkellner.com>:
> >>>
> >>>> Formulas for occuMulti follow the same standards as normal R formulas.
> >>>> So if you want to model the effect of two covariates on one parameter, the
> >>>> relevant formula would be '~var1 + var2'.
> >>>>
> >>>> In a normal occupancy model you only have two 'submodels', one for
> >>>> detection and one for occupancy. But for this model you have >2.
> >>>> Specifically, you have a submodel for every natural parameter (i.e. 'f'
> >>>> parameter) associated with occupancy, and one detection model per species.
> >>>> When you have two species, there are 3 f parameters (corresponding to
> >>>> species 1, species 2, and the species1:species2 interaction) associated
> >>>> with occupancy, hence the requirement for 3 formulas that you see. But each
> >>>> formula/submodel can have multiple covariates associated with it, as
> >>>> specified above.
> >>>>
> >>>> If you look further down in the example for occuMulti, under #update,
> >>>> you will see an example of this. Also, see the attached vignette for a more
> >>>> detailed overview of the function. Results from this model can be tricky to
> >>>> interpret and it is important to have a good understanding of what each
> >>>> natural parameter represents before trying to make conclusions. I'd
> >>>> recommend reading the Rota 2016 paper and, if possible, Chapter 8 in Kéry &
> >>>> Royle's Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology Vol 2.
> >>>>
> >>>> Ken
> >>>>
> >>>> On Tue, Nov 22, 2022 at 11:52:08AM -0800, D. Blaise wrote:
> >>>> > Good evening,
> >>>> >
> >>>> > I study the interaction between grazing species, before more
> >>>> complicate
> >>>> > models I first will do a model with two species.
> >>>> >
> >>>> > Formatting data into the unmarkedframe is easy,
> >>>> > but I do not understand some things following, I think it's because I
> >>>> only
> >>>> > have experience with Occu (for single species), which is much
> >>>> different.
> >>>> >
> >>>> > I copy below with questions;
> >>>> > umf <- unmarkedFrameOccuMulti(listo,siteCovs = covs,obsCovs = NULL)
> >>>> > summary(umf)
> >>>> >
> >>>> >
> >>>> >
> >>>> >
> >>>> >
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *95 sites2 species: sp1 sp2 Maximum number of observations per site:
> >>>> 11
> >>>> > Mean number of observations per site:sp1: 9.71578947368421 sp2:
> >>>> > 9.71578947368421 Sites with at least one detection:sp1: 63 sp2: 29
> >>>> *
> >>>> > etc.
> >>>> >
> >>>> > Then I need to provide 'detformulas' and 'stateformulas' but I find
> >>>> it
> >>>> > confusing:
> >>>> > I have 4 site variables and I want to study effect of variables on
> >>>> > (co-)occupancy, I have no detection variables (for now).
> >>>> > so intuition tells me:
> >>>> >
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *occForm <- c('~var1','~var2','~var3','~var4')detForm <-
> >>>> c('~1','~1`)*Which
> >>>> > is the variables for occupancy, and no detection variable for either
> >>>> > species (2x ~1)
> >>>> > But function documentation says:
> >>>> > # Length should match number/order of columns in fDesign
> >>>> > so
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *> fm <- occuMulti(detForm,occForm,umf) Error in .local(umf, ...) : 3
> >>>> > formulas are required in stateformulas list *
> >>>> >
> >>>> > For me:
> >>>> > > umf[@]fDesign
> >>>> > f1[sp1] f2[sp2] f3[sp1:sp2]
> >>>> > psi[11] 1 1 1
> >>>> > psi[10] 1 0 0
> >>>> > psi[01] 0 1 0
> >>>> > psi[00] 0 0 0
> >>>> > So what is the meaning of this? That I can only include 3 site
> >>>> covariates?
> >>>> > If I do this, code runs, despite warning for +20 missing detection
> >>>> sites:
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *occForm <- c('~var1','~var2','~var3')detForm <- c('~1','~1`)*
> >>>> >
> >>>> > But even now I do not have all covariates I want in model, estimates
> >>>> seem
> >>>> > 'incomplete'?
> >>>> > *Occupancy (logit-scale):*
> >>>> > * Estimate SE z
> >>>>
> >>>> > P(>|z|)*
> >>>> > *[sp1] (Intercept) 0.8492 0.8968 0.947 0.3436*
> >>>> > I think this is occupancy estimate just for SP1, without variables or
> >>>> > interaction with SP2?
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *[sp1] var1 -0.0021 0.0112 -0.188
> >>>> 0.8511*Ok,
> >>>> > but where are estimates for SP1 in relation to var2 and var3?
> >>>> > *[sp2] (Intercept) 2.4249 6.3518 0.382 0.7026*
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *[sp2] var2 -2.5174 4.0836 -0.616
> >>>> 0.5376*Where
> >>>> > are estimates for SP2 in relation to var1 and var3?
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *[sp1:sp2] (Intercept) -8.6237 5.8416 -1.476 0.1399*I think
> >>>> this
> >>>> > is estimate of the relation between species regarding their occupancy
> >>>> > estimates? (neg interaction estimate, but non-significant)
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *[sp1:sp2] var3 5.9214 3.5237 1.680
> >>>> 0.0929*Where are
> >>>> > estimates for relation between species in regard to var1 and var2?
> >>>> > *Detection (logit-scale):*
> >>>> > * Estimate SE z P(>|z|)*
> >>>> > *[sp1] (Intercept) -1.23 0.106 -11.59 4.68e-31*
> >>>> >
> >>>> > *[sp2] (Intercept) -1.23 0.154 -7.98 1.42e-15*Not sure what these
> >>>> mean
> >>>> > when I do not include observation covariates.
> >>>> >
> >>>> > I want to thank greatly anyone who could give help on interpretation,
> >>>> I
> >>>> > cannot find much information about occuMulti online, besides function
> >>>> > documentation.
